newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Eurobourses weak despite BT deal, dlr firms.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Eurobourses weak despite BT deal, dlr firms.

text.p: European bourses ended flat or weaker on Monday with London down half a percent despite a jump in British Telecom shares following news of its planned $20 billion merger with America's MCI Communications.
On the currency markets, the dollar regained some lost ground against the yen towards the end of the afternoon after earlier drifting gradually down towards 113 yen.
Dealers said trade was muted ahead of Tuesday's U.S. presidential elections with a victory for incumbent Bill Clinton already widely priced into the market.
In New York the Dow Industrial Average was up slightly as European equity trading ended.
Leading London stocks lost ground as political worries and weak futures prices trampled enthusiasm for the BT/MCI merger.
The FTSE 100 share index rose as high as 3,956.2 points in early trade as BT and other telecom shares soared on the news of the record trans-Atlantic deal.

But weak FTSE futures prices, worries about a possible Democrat sweep of the U.S. elections and the increasingly uncertain British political landscape knocked the gloss off the market and the FTSE 100 closed 20.4 points lower at 3,928.1.
BT shares closed at 372 pence, down from the day's high of 392 but still 22 pence up on Friday's closing price.

Traders said inflation-wary investors were increasingly concerned that a landslide victory for U.S. President Bill Clinton's Democrats could unleash fears of a wave of tax and spend policies and provoke a market rout.
"We could get a very nasty bout of profit-taking on Wall Street so it's time to play safe," the dealer said.

In Frankfurt, German shares ended bourse trade down but slightly off the day's lows. Dealers said the market had been catching up with Friday's late profit-taking. The 30-share DAX index ended down 11.39 points at 2,671.86.
One bright spot was mixed utility Viag AG, BT's partner in Germany. Its shares rose on news of the BT/MCI merger plan. In post-bourse electronic trading german shares firmed somewhat.

In Paris, trading was lacklustre though French shares managed to close in positive ground after spending much of the day in loss. Traders said the market was drifting and heavily influenced by U.S. market activity on the eve of the presidential poll.
Meanwhile, the dollar was pushed up to session highs against the yen in late trade but dealers said the markets were muted.
By 1645 GMT, the dollar was trading at 113.95 yen against a session low of 113.04 and 113.40 late Friday.
"There has not been a lot going on," said Alan Collins, head of technical analysis at Merita Bank in London. "There has not even been that much interest to take positions ahead of the election."
"I don't really see much impact from the presidential element," added Andrew Chaveriat, analyst at Paribas in London.
"It looks like we could see some concern on the bond market, which might be negative for the dollar, if the House of Representatives is swinging back to the Democrats."
But analysts noted that both parties were committed to a balanced budget and the president was likely to temper any straying from fiscal prudence.
CURRENCIES AT 1645 GMT
The dollar was trading at 1.5147 marks and 113.95 yen compared with late Friday's 1.5183 marks and 113.40 yen. STOCKS MARKETS CLOSING INDICES
The Financial Times-Stock Exchange index of 100 leading British shares ended 20.4 points lower at 3,928.1.
In Paris, the CAC-40 share index finished up 1.64 at 2,142.15.
The 30-share DAX index in Frankfurt closed down 11.39 at 2,671.86.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold closed at $379.10 compared with $377.65 at the London close on Friday. Silver ended up four cents at $4.82.
